items.title: Kein Ende im Streit um den Spritpreisdeckel
items.subtitle: Lange hat die Koalition um den Spritpreisdeckel gerungen.
items.feedText: Die SPD verhinderte eine erste Fassung. Die zweite enthält Ausnahmen und Zugeständnisse an die Tankwirtschaft. Das sorgt jetzt für neuen Ärger in der Koalition.
items.body:
# Kein Ende im Streit um den Spritpreisdeckel

Die Tankstellenpreise sind in den letzten Tagen gesunken . Ob und wie lange das so bleibt, lässt sich kaum seriös sagen. Die Bundesregierung will deshalb vorsorgen. Derzeit gilt noch der Tankrabatt . Ab 1. Januar soll ein befristeter Spritpreisdeckel übernehmen. Wie der aussieht, darum wurde hart gerungen. Ein neuer Entwurf, der laut Ministeriumskreisen seit wenigen Tagen abgestimmt wird, sollte den Streit zwischen SPD und Union befrieden. Er soll am 2. Dezember verabschiedet werden. Ob es dazu kommt, ist aber nach BR24-Informationen offen.

- Zum Artikel: Spritpreisdeckel - Aufatmen an der Tanke oder Versorgungsengpass?
## Worum geht es?

Ein Koalitionsausschuss hatte sich im September auf einen Spritpreisdeckel ab Januar geeinigt. Der liegt in der Verantwortung von Bundeswirtschaftsministerin Katherina Reiche (CDU). Doch sie hält ihn "für den falschen Weg". Reiches Sorge: dass der Spritpreisdeckel für Versorgungsengpässe mit Kraftstoff sorgen könnte, wenn er zu niedrig angesetzt wird und das Geschäft unwirtschaftlich wird.

Den Gesetzentwurf und eine Verordnung musste sie trotzdem liefern. Gegen den lief dann die SPD Sturm. Die Hürden seien viel zu hoch , als dass er je zum Einsatz kommen könnte, lautete die Kritik. Die zweite Fassung entstand nach dem Koalitionsausschuss letzte Woche.

## So könnte der neue Spritpreisdeckel aussehen

Der neue Entwurf für einen Deckel liegt BR24 vor. Er sieht vor, dass es einen bundesweiten Höchstpreis gibt, der sich an den Großhandelspreisen der in den letzten drei Tagen teuersten von insgesamt elf Tanklagerregionen in Deutschland orientiert. Dazu kommt eine Marge für die Tankstellen, die in der Berechnung so hoch angesetzt ist, dass der Deckel nur bei zehn Prozent die Marge beschneiden würde.

Außerdem sollen die Länder vom bundesweiten Höchstpreis nach oben oder unten abweichen dürfen, weil die Kosten regional variieren. Und eine Sonderregelung sieht vor, dass Autobahntankstellen grundsätzlich vom Höchstpreis ausgenommen sind.

## Experten bezweifeln die Deckelwirksamkeit

Der ADAC geht davon aus, "dass der Preisdeckel wahrscheinlich eher zu punktuellen Begrenzungen einzelner regionaler und tageszeitlicher Preisspitzen führen wird, vor allem nach der täglichen Preiserhöhung um 12.00 Uhr". Ob das Instrument tatsächlich zu spürbaren Preissenkungen führe, bleibe abzuwarten.

Steffen Bukold von EnergyComment erklärt der dpa: "Sie wird die Tankstellenpreise, abgesehen vom 12.00-Uhr-Preissprung, nicht deckeln können, da sie den Interessen der Kraftstoffanbieter viel zu weit entgegenkommt." Der Entwurf sei "zahnlos".

## Spritpreisdeckel: Ärger in der SPD

Vorsichtige Kritik kommt von SPD-Fraktionschef Matthias Miersch am Mittwoch: "Der Spritpreisdeckel ist für uns ein Instrument, das mit Zähnen versehen werden muss." Deutlicher wird sein Fraktionskollege: "Auch der überarbeitete Entwurf von Frau Reiche ist noch kein wirksamer Spritpreisdeckel", sagt Michael Schrodi, Bayern-SPD-Mitglied und Parlamentarischer Staatssekretär im Finanzministerium, zu BR24. "Ein Preisdeckel, der an der Zapfsäule kaum etwas verändert, erfüllt seinen Zweck nicht." Schrodi hält "gar nichts" von der Ausnahme für Autobahntankstellen und nicht von der Erlaubnis für Bundesländer, vom Höchstpreis abzuweichen.

## Befürchtung: Statt Entlastung hohe Preise

Experten hatten bereits vor Tanktourismus zwischen den Bundesländern gewarnt. Schrodi kritisiert auch die Festsetzung des maximalen Literpreises: Es sei nicht nachvollziehbar, warum ausgerechnet der höchste regionale Großhandelspreis die Grundlage für den bundesweiten Preisdeckel bilden soll. "Damit wird von vornherein ein unnötig hohes Preisniveau zugrunde gelegt." Ähnlich die Berechnung der Margen für die Tankstellen: "Wenn die erlaubten Aufschläge sogar über den zuletzt tatsächlich erzielten durchschnittlichen Margen liegen, wird der Deckel keine Wirkung zeigen." Seine Befürchtung: keine Entlastungen, nur überhöhte Preise.

## CSU: Am Ende muss eine echte Entlastung herauskommen

Die CSU im Bundestag ist vorsichtig: "Für uns steht fest: Die Versorgungssicherheit muss garantiert und die regionalen Gegebenheiten müssen berücksichtigt werden – und am Ende muss eine echte Entlastung für die Menschen an der Zapfsäule dabei herauskommen", erklärt Landesgruppenchef Alexander Hoffmann auf Anfrage von BR24.

Nach Berechnungen des "Handelsblatts" hätte der geplante Spritpreisdeckel die Preise von April bis November um sieben Cent pro Liter gesenkt, wenn er schon gegolten hätte. Das Bundeswirtschaftsministerium erklärt: "Der Spritpreisdeckel ist kein Tankrabatt im neuen Gewand. Er ist keine Entlastungsmaßnahme." Wer gezielt finanziell entlasten wolle, brauche andere Maßnahmen. Etwa "eine einkommensabhängige Zahlung auf das Konto von Bürgerinnen und Bürger". Damit spielt Reiche den Ball zurück an Finanzminister Lars Klingbeil von der SPD.

Deutlich wird: Der Spritpreisdeckel ist immer noch nicht in der Regierung geeint. Und es ist unklar, ob das bis zur nächsten Kabinettssitzung gelingt. Viel Zeit bis zum 1. Januar bleibt nicht mehr.

Das ist die Europäische Perspektive bei BR24.

"Hier ist Bayern": Der BR24 Newsletter informiert Sie immer montags bis freitags zum Feierabend über das Wichtigste vom Tag auf einen Blick – kompakt und direkt in Ihrem privaten Postfach. Hier geht’s zur Anmeldung!

items.body:
## STUDIO MASSIMO EMBEDS TIMBER OFFICE INTO DUTCH HEATHLAND

Situated on the Tafelberg heath in Blaricum, east of **[Amsterdam](https://www.designboom.com/tag/architecture-in-the-netherlands/)**, Office by Nature, Tafelberg is a 1,120-sqm**[timber](https://www.designboom.com/tag/wood-and-timber-architecture/) [office](https://www.designboom.com/tag/where-people-work/)**designed by Studio Massimo. Built within a protected glacial landscape and drinking-water catchment area, the project required low-impact construction to protect the surrounding soil. Taking structural and formal cues from the regional plaggenhut, a traditional earthen-walled dwelling topped with a sod roof, the building merges directly with the terrain. The ground slopes upward without an edge or material break to form a walkable living**[roof](https://www.designboom.com/tag/rooftop-architecture-and-design/)** planted with more than one hundred native, organically grown species.

Each elevation responds to its orientation. On the north side facing the road, the planted slope terminates at a mortarless retaining wall of stacked reclaimed paving tiles, punctuated only by a timber entrance door. The east and west gables are clad in untreated poplar bark shingles, a timber-industry byproduct that weathers from umber to silver-gray, while six-meter-wide sliding glass doors on the south facade open the workspaces directly onto the heath.

the office seen from the Tafelberg heath | all images ©Riccardo De Vecchi

## CLT STRUCTURE and RED GRANDIS INTERIORS COMPLETE BUILDING

Constructed from a laminated timber and cross-laminated timber (CLT) frame insulated with wood fiber, the interior is finished in a continuous palette of Red Grandis timber across walls, ceilings, doors, and joinery, with ventilation slots milled directly into the wood panels to eliminate visible grilles. A seven-meter-high central hall illuminated by an overhead skylight anchors the plan, floored in terrazzo aggregate containing split Kunrader stone from South Limburg, the same stone used for the exterior plinth. The design studio integrates a rainwater harvesting system that treats and reuses runoff for roof irrigation and toilets, guiding water down the south facade via reused crane chains, where each bay incorporates a secondary, higher overflow chain that discharges only when gutters require clearing. Outside, a sunken seating area built from reclaimed mooring poles and glacial boulders sits within untamed native planting.

items.title: Berufswahl und KI: Hat das Handwerk wieder goldenen Boden?
items.subtitle: Immer mehr Studenten verlassen die Hochschulen, weil sie wegen KI um ihre Berufschancen bangen, und erlernen ein Handwerk.

items.body:
# Ist es klug, ein Handwerk zu lernen statt zu studieren?

Handwerk, sagte man lange, hat goldenen Boden. Dann kam die Akademisierung von allem. Und jetzt geht die Furcht vor der Künstlichen Intelligenz um. Junge Leute und ihre Eltern fragen seit einiger Zeit, welche Berufe denn noch sicher davor seien, durch KI ersetzt zu werden.

So läuft es allerdings seit Jahrzehnten schon. Mal war es die Botschaft, Lehrer würden der Demographie halber kaum mehr eingestellt. Dann hieß es, eine Zukunft hätten nur noch Betriebswirtschaftler und Informatiker, vielleicht noch Maschinenbauer. Erleichtert wurde zur Kenntnis genommen, dass die Unternehmensberatungen auch Physiker und Musikwissenschaftler einstellten, denn denen war auch gesagt worden, ihr Studium sei eine berufliche Sackgasse.

Oder es wurde das Jurastudium empfohlen, weil man damit immerhin alles Mögliche werden könne: Richterin, Anwalt oder Politiker. Immer aber wurde gesagt, so viele, wie im Hörsaal säßen, brauche man gar nicht, und stets fanden die meisten einen Beruf.

### Enorme Substitutionsphantasien

Jetzt ist freilich die Situation eine andere. Es heißt nicht, so viele Historiker, Anwälte, Informatiker brauche niemand, es heißt, man brauche sie gar nicht mehr. Mit der KI gehen enorme Substitutionsphantasien einher. Denn was kann sie nicht? Wer einwirft, die KI habe kein Bewusstsein, zieht die Gegenfrage auf sich, ob für Marken- und für Mietrecht, für Riemanns Vermutung und für Drehbücher, die vom ZDF verfilmt werden, denn Bewusstsein benötigt wird.

Philosophische Erwägungen und solche zu den gesamtgesellschaftlichen Folgen der KI können denjenigen, die sich überlegen, welchen Studien- und Berufsweg sie einschlagen sollen, gleichgültig sein. Es stellen sich praktische Fragen. Schon gibt es die ersten Berichte über Absolventen aus Oxford, die Klempnerin geworden sind, angehende Medizinerinnen, die ihr Studium für eine Schreinerlehre abgebrochen haben. Denn was die KI aller Robotik zum Trotz einstweilen noch nicht kann, ist Tafelspitz zubereiten, Schränke tischlern, Babys wickeln, Dachrinnen anbringen, Hamlet spielen oder Bratsche.

Die Maschine, einst als Gerät gedacht, das uns körperliche Arbeit erspart, erfährt im Höhepunkt ihrer Produktivität eine Grenze ironischerweise an bestimmten Arten solcher intelligenten Tätigkeit mit Augen und Händen. Das enthält auch einen Hinweis für die Universitäten. Sie könnten, Fach für Fach, ihre Lehrprogramme daraufhin durchmustern, was der Maschine überlassen werden kann, und sich auf den Rest sowie die Handhabung der Maschine KI konzentrieren. Der Rest wird je nach Disziplin unterschiedlich groß sein, so wie es unterschiedliche Antworten darauf gibt, wie viele Anwälte und wie viele Köche die Menschheit benötigt.

Die Geschichte mit dem Handwerker Rocky, die gerade im Boxerfilm-Film „I Play Rocky“ erzählt wird, belegt übrigens, dass die Menschheit etwas Überraschendes, das sie unterhält, immer benötigt. Und sei es ein Gedanke.

items.title: Only one in five of Kazakhstan's endemic plants has data for initial range screening
items.subtitle: Kazakhstan has hundreds of plant species found nowhere else in the world.
items.feedText: Many have been known to botanists for decades, described in floristic publications and held in herbarium collections. Yet knowing that a plant exists is different from having the information needed to judge its prospects for survival.
items.body:
# Only one in five of Kazakhstan's endemic plants has data for initial range screening

November 25, 2026

## Only one in five of Kazakhstan's endemic plants has data for initial range screening

edited by Swati Mestri , reviewed by Robert Egan

Swati Mestri

Scientific Editor

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:

fact-checked

peer-reviewed publication

trusted source

proofread

Kazakhstan has hundreds of plant species found nowhere else in the world. Many have been known to botanists for decades, described in floristic publications and held in herbarium collections. Yet knowing that a plant exists is different from having the information needed to judge its prospects for survival.

Researchers at the Institute of Botany and Phytointroduction in Almaty measured that difference.

Their study begins with a national checklist of 451 endemic vascular plant taxa. Taxa that needed taxonomic clarification or reassessment of an existing conservation status were handled separately, leaving 419. For these, the team used occurrence records from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), checked them manually and combined them with geographical information from Kazakhstan's floristic regionalization.

The research is published in the Biodiversity Data Journal .

## Most taxa lack usable location data

The results show a wide gap between botanical knowledge and accessible spatial data. For 210 taxa, 50.1% of those screened, the data set contained no usable georeferenced records. A further 113 were represented by only one or two suitable localities, and five had records that could not produce an informative range estimate. In total, 328 taxa (78.3%) require more work on their occurrence data. Only 91 of the 419 taxa (21.7%) had enough occurrence data for preliminary screening of their extent of occurrence (EOO). This is the area enclosed by a species' outermost known records.

"Kazakhstan has a long history of botanical research, and much of what we know about its endemic plants is preserved in herbarium collections, scientific publications and field records. The problem is that this knowledge is not always available in a form we can use for modern conservation assessments. In many cases, we need to recover and organize existing information before collecting new data," explains Alexander Dubynin, lead author of the study.

The method separates plants whose records allow initial range calculations from those that need coordinate corrections, additional locality information or searches of herbarium collections and botanical literature.

Among the 91 screenable taxa, 66 had calculated geographical ranges below 20,000 km² (7,700 square miles), a threshold relevant to criterion B1 of the IUCN Red List. Such figures justify closer investigation but cannot establish that a species is threatened. Population trends, habitat loss, fragmentation and the number of locations must also be considered. The authors therefore treat data readiness, range restriction and extinction risk as separate questions.

## Recovering knowledge from existing collections

A lack of digital records does not necessarily mean a lack of botanical knowledge. Global databases hold only part of what botanists know, and records in national herbaria, field notebooks, regional publications and institutional archives may never have reached them. Some of the missing information may already exist, awaiting verification and digitization.

- Work in a herbarium. Credit: Alexander V. Dubynin.
- Regel's tulip (Tulipa regelii). Credit: Alexander V. Dubynin.
- Screening workflow for the 419 taxa in the common spatial-data screening set. Spatial-data status is evaluated independently from point-derived and floristic range signals. Point-screenable taxa proceed to assessment-specific evidence review before formal IUCN Red List assessment. Credit: Dubynin et al., 2026
The study provides a basis for organizing this work across Kazakhstan's endemic flora. It also offers an approach that could be applied in other regions where decades of botanical research have yet to be fully reflected in the data available for biodiversity conservation.

Publication details

Alexander Dubynin et al., From occurrence records to Red List assessment: screening spatial-data readiness of Kazakhstan's endemic vascular plants, Biodiversity Data Journal (2026). DOI: 10.3897/bdj.14.e193212

Journal information: Biodiversity Data Journal

items.body:
# ‘Blade Runner 2099’ cast praise the incredible set designs that brought the sci-fi universe to life: ‘it was all so well-realized’ (interview)

The most obvious change in this depressing dystopia is that replicants are running the LA show after some unmentionable ecological disaster and humans are now the ones relegated to underclass citizens.

Starring Michelle Yeoh as a replicant cop named Olwen whose life clock is running out and Hunter Schafer as Cora, a desperate human posing as a replicant blade runner, "Blade Runner 2099" unties these two in a mystery revolving around a rogue blade runner and a deadly secret that might cause their city to implode.

We connected with three of the sci-fi show’s main co-stars, Matthew Needham ("House of the Dragon"), Lewis Gribben ("T2 Trainspotting") and Dimitri Abold ("Love Addicts") to hear more about working with creator/showrunner Silka Louisa, and immersing themselves in " Blade Runner 2099's " vivid futuristic worldbuilding.

"For me it's a lot simpler than egos because he's such a goal-oriented person and all of his stuff has such a police procedural quality to it," Needham tells SPACE regarding his role as Yahya, an emotionless replicant who despises all humans.

"It was really fun to just follow what Silka [Louisa] did. She wrote this great, really exciting mystery thriller, and I just got to play in that.”

Scottish actor Gribben portrays Cora's ailing younger brother Elias, who has compromised mobility and a rocky relationship with his overprotective sister.

"I've played a few characters that were fairly vulnerable or insular," he notes. "Then seeing the journey of this character grow in strength and confidence and feel like becoming his own man was so compelling to me. It’s almost a relationship that falls apart between brother and sister, and that's fascinating to me because that’s such a cool dynamic you don’t always really see in television shows. That was quite interesting and made me want to try and be in it."

As Bebeto, a doctor, veteran of the replicants vs. humans war, and a black-market dealer helping his species procure IDs and passports off-world, Abold enjoyed exploring the many facets of his character.

"Much like Matthew and Lewis, for me it was the journey that Bebeto goes on," Abold adds. "Starting out as someone who’s so hopeful and has to try and scrape up the last dregs of hope as things start falling apart. Being subject to circumstances like that inherently make for an interesting story arc and story in general. Throwing myself into that, especially after how well Silka crafted the story and script, was something I was totally ready for."

"Blade Runner 2099’s" sets and locations feature detailed production design that allowed the actors to experience a seamless transition into the complex shoot.

"For me and Dimitri, our first day was in Bebeto’s apartment, and it was all so well-realized,” Gribben recalls.

"You saw all the gadgets because obviously Bebeto was a bit of a tinkerer of a character and had lots of machinery and works and stuff. It took up about 70% of the acting, and we just had to come with compelling conviction. It made it so easy. When you audition for these things, you feel like you have to act more because you’re in a blue screen vacuum. But then you’re there, and it’s so visually well created like that, it made it so easy to be immersed in it."

items.title: Rechtsextremistische Chatgruppe "Terror 18" - Drei Teenager unter Terrorverdacht festgenommen - zwei Beschuldigte wieder auf freiem Fuß
items.subtitle: Nach der Festnahme von drei mutmaßlichen Mitgliedern einer rechtsextremistischen Terrorgruppe sind zwei der Beschuldigten wieder auf freiem Fuß.
items.feedText: Ein Ermittlungsrichter am Amtsgericht Helmstedt sowie sein Amtskollege am Bundesgerichtshof in Karlsruhe setzten die Haftbefehle unter Auflagen außer Vollzug, wie eine Sprecherin der Bundesanwaltschaft mitteilte.
items.body:
# Rechtsextremistische Chatgruppe "Terror 18" - Drei Teenager unter Terrorverdacht festgenommen - zwei Beschuldigte wieder auf freiem Fuß

## Bereits im Oktober Festnahmen

Die Bundesanwaltschaft (dpa / Christoph Schmidt) Die dritte Haftvorführung dauerte am frühen Abend noch an. Die Bundesanwaltschaft wirft den Jugendlichen im Alter von 14 bis 15 Jahren die Mitgliedschaft in einer terroristischen Vereinigung vor. Deren Ziel sei es gewesen, im Namen der rechtsradikalen Chatgruppe "Terror 18" schwerste Straftaten durchzuführen. Die Beschuldigten wurden am Morgen in mehreren Bundesländern gefasst. Laut Bundesanwaltschaft handelt es sich um Jugendliche aus Brandenburg, Niedersachsen und Schleswig-Holstein. Sie verbinde die tiefe Ablehnung der politischen und demokratischen Verhältnisse in Deutschland, hieß es. Die Vereinigung habe sich zum Ziel gesetzt, schwerste Straftaten zu begehen, insbesondere Brandstiftungen und Gewalttaten bis hin zu gezielten Tötungen von Ausländern und politischen Gegnern. Unter anderem soll die Gruppe einen Brandanschlag auf eine Flüchtlingsunterkunft im niedersächsischen Winsen (Luhe) geplant haben. Bereits im Oktober Festnahmen In mehreren Bundesländern fanden Durchsuchungen statt. Diese richteten sich nach Angaben der Bundesanwaltschaft auch gegen vier weitere Verdächtige im Alter von 14 bis 16 Jahren, die auf freiem Fuß sind. Ihnen werde teils die Unterstützung der terroristischen Vereinigung, teils die Nichtanzeige geplanter Straftaten vorgeworfen. Bereits im Oktober waren drei mutmaßliche Gruppenmitglieder in Norddeutschland festgenommen worden. Diese Nachricht wurde am 25.11.2026 im Programm Deutschlandfunk gesendet.

items.body:
MARK SYKES/SPL/Alamy

There is a story, possibly apocryphal, that when the mathematician G. H. Hardy was about to undertake a dangerous sea voyage, he sent a postcard to a colleague declaring “I have solved the Riemann hypothesis”. Hardy, a staunch atheist, joked that this would prevent his ship from sinking, as God would never let him claim the credit for such a major result without revealing the details of his proof.

Hardy would probably be both astonished and aghast that [we now have what seems to be a proof of the Riemann hypothesis](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2600134-anthropic-mathematician-claims-ai-assisted-proof-of-the-riemann-hypothesis/), a problem that has vexed mathematicians since the 19th century, but that no one yet understands it. The consensus among mathematicians is that the proof, produced with the aid of AI, will hold, but that it will take much more work to make it comprehensible to humans.

However you feel about AI, this is a watershed moment, and one that demonstrates just how little we still understand about the capabilities of the technology. As recently as last month, leading mathematician Terence Tao speculated that AI would eventually solve the Riemann hypothesis, but that it may not happen before 2050. Now, some mathematicians are considering whether their hardest and most infamous remaining problems could be settled within months. In a year that has left mathematicians reeling, this may be the knock-out blow.

> This is a watershed moment, and it shows just how little we understand about AI’s abilities

For non-mathematicians, the fall of the Riemann hypothesis is harder to interpret. In the past year, AI has seen incredible advances in both maths and coding, but it is perhaps no coincidence that in these arenas, with nothing more than computer code, answers can swiftly be checked and iterated upon, allowing for rapid improvement. When it comes to other human endeavours though, from art to zoology, such verification is far harder, involving either the messy physical world, or unknowable human taste – or both. Whether this verification gap can be closed may become the biggest question of our age. Answers on a postcard, please.

items.subtitle: A novel molecular imaging approach that measures beta-cell mass in the pancreas can offer valuable insights into the progression of type 1 diabetes…

items.body:
# PET/CT imaging provides new insights into type 1 diabetes progression

## PET/CT imaging provides new insights into type 1 diabetes progression

edited by Gaby Clark , reviewed by Andrew Zinin

Gaby Clark

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:

fact-checked

peer-reviewed publication

trusted source

proofread

A novel molecular imaging approach that measures beta-cell mass in the pancreas can offer valuable insights into the progression of type 1 diabetes, according to new research published in the Journal of Nuclear Medicine . The study found that individuals who have had type 1 diabetes for less than seven years have higher total beta-cell mass and function, larger pancreatic volume and lower intrapancreatic fat compared to those who have had the disease for longer. This valuable information, paired with functional tests, has the potential to significantly improve clinical trials of new therapeutic interventions.

Globally, more than 9.5 million people live with type 1 diabetes. In this chronic disease, pancreatic beta cells are destroyed over time, leading to an insulin deficiency and thereby hyperglycemia.

"Not all beta cells will be destroyed in type 1 diabetes, but the exact timing and fate of beta-cell loss are still unknown," said Sevilay Tokgöz, Ph.D., a postdoctoral researcher at Radboud University Medical Center in Nijmegen, the Netherlands. "A better understanding of this process is required to develop therapeutic strategies to halt disease progression."

In the study, Tokgöz and colleagues measured total beta-cell mass using ⁶⁸Ga-NODAGA-exendin-4 PET/CT imaging, an approach that targets GLP-1 receptors that are highly expressed on beta cells. Data from 16 individuals with short-duration type 1 diabetes (less than seven years) and 10 with long-duration type 1 diabetes (more than seven years) were analyzed. Participants underwent ⁶⁸Ga-NODAGA-exendin-4 PET/CT and a mixed-meal tolerance test to determine total beta-cell mass and function, respectively. Intrapancreatic fat deposition and pancreatic volume were derived from CT.

Total beta-cell mass and function were higher in individuals with short-duration type 1 diabetes compared with those with long-duration type 1 diabetes. Larger pancreatic volume and lower intrapancreatic fat deposition were also observed in individuals with short-duration type 1 diabetes compared with the long-duration group. Together, these findings provide new insights into the relationship between beta-cell mass, function and disease duration.

"These findings are highly relevant in regard to the development of therapies aimed at restoring beta-cell function or preserving beta-cell mass," said Tokgöz. "They may aid in more precise estimates of treatment effects and improve the logistics of clinical trials, and in the future could identify individuals who may benefit from therapeutic interventions."

Publication details

Sevilay Tokgöz et al., β-Cell Mass and Function, Pancreatic Volume, and Fat Differences Between Short- and Long-Duration Type 1 Diabetes: A Detailed PET/CT Imaging Study, Journal of Nuclear Medicine (2026). DOI: 10.2967/jnumed.126.272915

Nun wird an der Wall Street intensiv über eine unbequeme Frage diskutiert: Was kann die Angst der Anleger jetzt stoppen?

items.title: Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains
items.subtitle: Nearly one in three older adults with dementia or other cognitive disorders takes potentially harmful medications that can worsen brain function an…
items.feedText: Despite encouraging progress over the past decade, researchers warn that medication-related harm remains a major and potentially preventable threat to healthy aging.
items.body:
# Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains

## Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains

Adults age 65 and older who have dementia or other cognitive disorders are particularly vulnerable to the harmful effects of medications used to treat anxiety, sleep disturbances, psychosis, and other conditions affecting the central nervous system.

Potential consequences include more emergency room visits, longer and more frequent hospital stays, declining mental health, and an increased risk of premature death.

New research from the University at Buffalo (UB) offers some encouraging news, however. Between 2011 and 2022, the proportion of older adults with cognitive disorders taking medications that could impair their cognitive function decreased significantly.

After analyzing data from 2,796 older adults with cognitive disorders who lived independently, researchers found that exposure to potentially inappropriate medications fell from 39.3% in 2011 to 29.3% in 2022.

"This is a population with some mental issues that relate to the central nervous system. These drugs also act on the central nervous system, so they can be too much for older adults if inappropriately used," says Haowen Hsu, PharmD, a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Pharmacy Practice at the School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences and first author of the study, published in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society .

Reducing the Risks of Common Prescription Drugs

Older adults who have spent years taking benzodiazepines such as Xanax for anxiety or sleep medications such as Ambien may benefit from a medically supervised reduction in dosage or gradual discontinuation. These medications can negatively affect cognitive function, balance, and coordination.

"A central word for patients in this age group is 'deprescribing,' which means, for example, removing inappropriate medications and decreasing the frequency or the dosage. In some cases, it means replacing the current medication with a milder alternative," Hsu says. "This is why it's so important for health care providers to work closely with community pharmacists and homecare nurses to optimize medication safety."

To identify potentially problematic drugs, the research team consulted the American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria, which identifies approximately 100 medications that may pose risks to older adults. The researchers then concentrated specifically on medications that could present additional dangers for people with diagnosed cognitive disorders.

Using data from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey, the team examined a sample representing approximately 29.7 million older Americans with cognitive disorders over the period from 2011 to 2022. They compared individuals prescribed at least one potentially inappropriate medication with those who had not received any of these drugs.

Medication Safety Has Improved, but Risks Remain

Although the study did not examine what caused the decline in exposure to potentially harmful medications, Hsu points to growing awareness among researchers and clinicians over the past two decades. The gradual but sustained improvement may reflect broader advances in geriatric medicine and efforts to make prescription drug use safer.

"We were happy to see the percentages of harm decline over that 11-year period," he says. "However, one-third of our target population is still exposed to these harmful medications, which isn't good."

Older adults, even those without cognitive disorders, are particularly susceptible to harmful drug interactions and inappropriate prescriptions. In some cases, these complications can increase the risk of death. These dangers are a central focus of Team Alice, an ongoing interdisciplinary research initiative at the University at Buffalo dedicated to medication safety.

A Preventable Death Inspires Change

Team Alice takes its name from Alice Brennan, who died in 2009 following a prescription for a muscle relaxant identified as potentially inappropriate under the Beers Criteria. The prescribing error went unrecognized within the health care system, and Brennan died following six weeks of preventable complications.

Her daughter, Mary Brennan-Taylor, shared her mother's experience with University at Buffalo researchers in the hope of bringing about systemic changes that would spare other patients and families from similar harm.

Hsu began the new study shortly after joining the university's pharmacy school and Team Alice, where he works in the UB Patient Safety Learning Laboratory.

"This work extends a series of national analyses our group has published on potentially inappropriate medications, quality of life, and health care use in older adults," says David Jacobs, PharmD, PhD, associate professor of pharmacy practice and a principal investigator on Team Alice.

"It is especially important as older adults with cognitive disorders are the least able to tolerate medications that worsen memory or thinking, yet nearly one in three are still receiving them. Most of these patients have a regular source of care so these medications can be identified and addressed with their care team."

Improving Medication Safety for Older Adults

Other contributors to the study included Team Alice's fellow principal investigators Ranjit Singh, MD, associate professor and interim chair of the Department of Family Medicine at UB's Jacobs School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, and Robert Wahler, PharmD, clinical associate professor of pharmacy practice.

Collin Clark, PharmD, clinical associate professor of pharmacy practice, and Steven Feuerstein, an information systems analyst at the Jacobs School, also contributed to the research.

items.body:
BERLIN. **Berufliche Schulen sollen jungen Menschen auch dann noch eine Perspektive eröffnen, wenn ihre bisherige Schullaufbahn von Misserfolgen und Brüchen geprägt war. Doch ausgerechnet in den Bildungsgängen, die Jugendliche ohne Ausbildungsplatz auf das Berufsleben vorbereiten, sind Lehrkräfte besonders mit Gewalt und hohen Fehlzeiten konfrontiert. Das geht aus einer bundesweiten Befragung von knapp 2.000 Lehrkräften durch den Bundesverband der Lehrkräfte für Berufsbildung (BvLB) hervor. Der Verband sieht die Ursachen vielfach in der Bildungsbiografie der Jugendlichen – und fordert Konsequenzen für die personelle Ausstattung der Schulen. Eine große Mehrheit der befragten Lehrkräfte wünscht sich auch ein konsequenteres Vorgehen gegen Schulabsentismus.**

Lust auf Schule? (Symbolfoto.) Foto: Shutterstock

Fast drei Viertel der befragten Lehrkräfte an beruflichen Schulen (73 Prozent) fühlen sich auf den Umgang mit Gewalt nicht ausreichend vorbereitet. Allerdings verteilen sich die Probleme höchst unterschiedlich auf die einzelnen Bildungsgänge. Während 61 Prozent der Befragten die Berufsvorbereitung als besonders von Gewalt betroffen nennen, sind es beim beruflichen Gymnasium lediglich vier Prozent. Zu den häufigsten Erscheinungsformen zählen nach Angaben der Lehrkräfte psychische Gewalt wie Beleidigungen und Mobbing, aber auch körperliche Auseinandersetzungen unter Schülerinnen und Schülern.

Das geht aus einer nun veröffentlichten Befragung des Bundesverbands der Lehrkräfte für Berufsbildung hervor, an der sich zwischen dem 12. April und dem 27. August dieses Jahres 1.969 Lehrkräfte an beruflichen Schulen aus 14 Bundesländern beteiligt haben. Die Ergebnisse sind zwar nicht repräsentativ, vermitteln aber ein breites Stimmungsbild aus der schulischen Praxis.

## „Lehrkräfte an beruflichen Schulen leisten täglich weit mehr als Unterricht – im Übergangsbereich ganz besonders“

Auch beim Schulabsentismus zeigen sich erhebliche Unterschiede zwischen den Bildungsgängen. 56 Prozent der Befragten nennen Berufsfachschulen als besonders von Fehlzeiten betroffen, 49 Prozent die Berufsvorbereitung. Schulabsentismus ist allerdings auch in der dualen Berufsausbildung ein Thema: 29 Prozent der befragten Lehrkräfte nennen die Berufsschule im dualen System als besonders betroffen. Damit berührt das Problem unmittelbar auch die Bemühungen um die Fachkräftesicherung. Regelmäßige Fehlzeiten gefährden den erfolgreichen Abschluss einer bereits begonnenen Ausbildung.

Die besondere Konzentration der Probleme im Übergangsbereich hat nach Einschätzung des BvLB wesentlich mit den Voraussetzungen zu tun, unter denen die Jugendlichen an die beruflichen Schulen kommen. In den entsprechenden Bildungsgängen werden junge Menschen ohne Ausbildungsplatz auf eine Berufsausbildung vorbereitet oder zu einem Hauptschulabschluss beziehungsweise einem mittleren Schulabschluss geführt. Für viele von ihnen ist dies die Möglichkeit, Versäumtes aus ihrer bisherigen Schullaufbahn nachzuholen und überhaupt erst die Voraussetzungen für eine Berufsausbildung zu erwerben.

Woher die Probleme kommen, die den Lehrkräften dabei begegnen, beschreiben die Befragten ebenfalls. Als wesentliche Einflussfaktoren nennen sie Schulmüdigkeit, negative Schulerfahrungen, familiäre Probleme und Überforderung. Die Ursachen für die Schwierigkeiten im Übergangsbereich liegen demnach vielfach in einer Zeit, in der die Jugendlichen noch gar keine berufliche Schule besuchten – und zum Teil außerhalb des Einflussbereichs von Schule überhaupt.

Für die Lehrkräfte bedeutet das, dass sie neben der fachlichen Qualifizierung der Jugendlichen auch daran arbeiten müssen, deren Bereitschaft zum Schulbesuch wiederherzustellen. Sie beraten, vermitteln in Konflikten und versuchen, Schülerinnen und Schülern mit geeigneten Unterstützungsangeboten die Rückkehr in einen geregelten Schulalltag zu ermöglichen. Gleichzeitig sollen sie fachliche Defizite aufarbeiten und die Jugendlichen auf die Anforderungen einer Ausbildung vorbereiten.

Wie groß der Förderbedarf aus Sicht der Lehrkräfte ist, zeigen weitere Ergebnisse der Befragung. 46 Prozent wünschen sich mehr Lernberatung, 30 Prozent eine stärkere Sprachförderung und 29 Prozent zusätzliche Förderstunden. Der BvLB verweist in diesem Zusammenhang auf die Bedeutung grundlegender Kompetenzen im Lesen, Schreiben und Rechnen sowie auf die sprachlichen Voraussetzungen für eine erfolgreiche Berufsausbildung. Der Übergangsbereich übernimmt damit auch Aufgaben, die eigentlich bereits in den allgemeinbildenden Schulen hätten erfüllt werden sollen.

Besonders groß ist der Bedarf an Unterstützung durch andere Professionen: 81 Prozent der befragten Lehrkräfte wünschen sich mehr Unterstützung durch Schulsozialarbeit oder Schulpsychologie. „Lehrkräfte an beruflichen Schulen leisten täglich weit mehr als Unterricht – im Übergangsbereich ganz besonders. Unsere Befragung zeigt aber auch: Diese vielfältigen Aufgaben sind ohne zusätzliche Unterstützung auf Dauer nicht zu bewältigen. Bund und Länder sind jetzt gemeinsam gefordert“, erklärt Christian Löffler, Leiter der Fachkommission für Schul- und Bildungspolitik im BvLB.

Der Verband fordert deshalb, multiprofessionelle Teams dauerhaft an den beruflichen Schulen zu etablieren. Schulsozialarbeit, Schulpsychologie und weitere pädagogische Fachkräfte müssten entsprechend dem tatsächlichen Bedarf zur Verfügung stehen. Unterstützungsstrukturen, die sich im Rahmen des Startchancen-Programms bewährten, müssten in die Regelfinanzierung übernommen werden – ausdrücklich auch an beruflichen Schulen.

Dass sich die Lehrkräfte nicht allein zusätzliche pädagogische Unterstützung wünschen, sondern auch eine verbindlichere Durchsetzung der Schulpflicht, zeigt ein weiteres Ergebnis der Befragung: 86 Prozent sprechen sich für Konsequenzen bei hohen Fehlzeiten aus. Fast die Hälfte (48 Prozent) wünscht sich mehr Unterstützung durch das Ordnungsamt.

items.body:
Gloria Steinem was booked up. There had been luncheons and interviews scheduled for the fall; a high-profile conversation with Katie Couric at 92NY and a prominent place in The New Yorker Festival’s lineup. She left appearances unfulfilled, interviews unaired, an essay unpublished and a forthcoming book. In short: Gloria Steinem was, at 92, far from done.

That energy is palpable in that very book, her memoir [An Unexpected Life](https://bookshop.org/p/books/an-unexpected-life-notes-from-a-hope-a-holic-gloria-steinem/4b7ec63a4c7acf42/?aid=132!), published on September 22, in which she states that she planned to live to at least 100. Although she was “older than [she] ever imagined,” mortality didn’t really cross her mind much. Any why would it, when she was also “happier than [she] ever imagined” and her calendar was bursting at the seams? Part memoir, part manifesto, part consciousness raising group, *An Unexpected Life* is a collection of essays in which Steinem reflects on her life, lays out her worldview and looks towards the future. And just as she was in life, on the page she radiates a matter-of-fact conviction and an unflinching clarity—the result of more than sixty years spent organizing a movement.

Her story begins long before she would become the most prominent face of second-wave feminism (although Steinem would reject this label), with a bruised childhood in Toledo, Ohio. She spent stretches of her young life on the road, until her father left when she was ten years old, leaving her in a rat-infested home caring for her increasingly mentally ill mother. With a childhood spent longing for warm kitchens and cookie cutter family units, it is striking that Steinem would grow up to spend so much of her adult life traveling around the country, more often than not living out of a suitcase. But even more formative than her earliest years, perhaps, was the time spent in India in her early 20s, an experience that would become the very foundation of her feminism.

Although mortality was far from Steinem’s mind, it is apparent in these pages that she was hyperaware of her legacy. “At my age, in this still hierarchical time, people often ask me if I’m ‘passing the torch,’” she wrote in her 1983 book [Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellion s](https://bookshop.org/p/books/outrageous-acts-and-everyday-rebellions-third-edition-gloria-steinem/753219586e6d55f1/?aid=132!). “I explain that I’m keeping my torch, thank you very much—and I’m using it to light the torches of others.”

She is doing just that in *An Unexpected Life*, a text bursting with a kind of hopeful exhilaration about what could be. “Nothing is more exciting than making the invisible visible. It’s like finding the end in a ball of yarn,” she wrote. “Pull on it, and gradually the whole of patriarchy unravels.” At times, she gets as literal as bullet-point lists on how to best organize a feminist movement. There are glimmers of the—often cited—shortcomings of the women’s movement that she was at the helm of herself. “Insist on multiracial women who represent the movement,” is one such takeaway of Steinem’s. “Otherwise, people will have a distorted view.” There is an added poignancy to the essays upon her passing; a book that is as much about her life as it is a handbook for movement building. “Whatever my story might be to other people,” Steinem wrote, “I hope something has ripple effects that I myself may never see.”

One such ripple effect concerns her beloved home, an apartment in a brownstone building on the Upper East Side of Manhattan. “If time and ingenuity allow,” Steinem wrote in the book’s prologue, “I hope to acquire the other floors in this house and leave this whole building as a refuge for diverse women who need a place to stay or just to meet.”

Steinem first moved into her apartment in 1968, together with a roommate. Throughout the years, the apartment grew not only in square footage but in function. The single unit became an entire floor, which became three floors. Her living room had been a meeting place for over fifty years, where she hosted gatherings and talking circles up until this very year. She held meeting on topics ranging from women’s health to misinformation in the media—a meeting in that very living room had led to the founding of *Ms. Magazine* in 1971. On September 3, Gloria’s Foundation announced that her brownstone would continue to be a feminist sanctuary; a place for women to father and organize, to discuss and seek shelter.

Lingering in the background of these pages is Steinem’s time in India. The years spent there upon graduating from Smith College made such a deep and lasting impression on Steinem, it not only ignited her activism but it is where her ideology was rooted throughout her life. In her final essay, published in [The New Yorker](https://www.newyorker.com/culture/life-and-letters/gloria-steinems-final-essay?utm_mailing=tny_nl_6667_daily_090326_utg9beo9c3&utm_source=nl&utm_brand=tny&utm_campaign=aud-dev&utm_medium=email&utm_content=tny_nl_6667_daily_090326_utg9beo9c3&cndid=64331124&utm_term=6667) following her passing, she wrote that it was where she realized that “white people were a very small minority in the world. In India, I got accustomed to, and began to value, racial diversity.” The open, nonviolent M.O. of Ghandi and his followers captivated her, perhaps not in the last place because she learned that his peace movement was once inspired by India’s women’s movement. “I think culturally women are drawn to nonviolence,” Steinem wrote in her final essay. “Probably because we are the major victims of violence, we become the major movers of peace.”

There is an odd comfort in having Gloria Steinem insist that it really, truly, *believe her*, has been worse.

items.body:
**Gibt es eigentlich moderne Synthesizer-Klassiker – also Synthesizer von heute, über die man auch in 20 oder 30 Jahren noch sprechen wird? Wir glauben: ja! Hier sind sechs aktuelle Synthesizer, die das Potenzial haben, zu echten Klassikern zu werden.**

## Table of Contents

- Moderne Synthesizer-Klassiker
- Arturia PolyBrute 12: Ausdrucksstärkster Analogsynthesizer aller Zeiten?
- Moog Mother-Serie: Semi-modular für alle
- ASM Hydrasynth: Der digitale Rebell
- Groove Synthesis 3rd Wave: Kompromisslos gut
- Expressive E Osmose: Die Keyboard-Revolution
- Teenage Engineering OP-1 (Field): Synthesizer-Klassiker und Designikone

## Moderne Synthesizer-Klassiker

Wenn von einem **Synthesizer-Klassiker** die Rede ist, denkt man natürlich zuerst an die analogen Legenden der 1970er und 1980er wie den Minimoog, Odyssey, Jupiter-8, Prophet-5, CS-80 oder OB-X. Auch unter den digitalen Synthesizern gibt es echte Klassiker vom DX7 über D-50, [M1](https://www.gearnews.de/synthesizer-klassiker-korg-m1/) und Wavestation bis zum [Virus](https://www.gearnews.de/access-virus-alternativen/), JP-8000 und microKORG.

Aber was ist mit den **Synthesizern von heute**? Sind sie nicht immer wieder neue Aufgüsse der gleichen Ideen? Verblassen sie nicht ausnahmslos gegenüber den Meilensteinen vergangener Jahrzehnte? Gibt es überhaupt moderne Synthesizer-Klassiker?

Yamaha CS-80: Einer der großen Synthesizer-Klassiker vergangener Jahrzehnte · Quelle: Yamaha

Wenn man sich die Flut an Klonen und Nachbauten von **Vintage-Synthesizern** ansieht, die derzeit ganz oben in den Verkaufscharts rangieren, könnte man meinen, es gehe heute nur noch darum, das Erbe der Vergangenheit zu verwalten. Doch der Eindruck täuscht. Auch unter den Synthesizern von heute gibt es einige, an die man sich garantiert auch in 10, 20 oder 30 Jahren noch erinnern wird – sei es wegen ihrer innovativen Ideen, ihres tollen Sounds oder einfach ihrer großen Beliebtheit.

Einige Kandidaten, bei denen wir uns gut vorstellen können, dass man sie eines Tages als **Synthesizer-Klassiker** bezeichnen wird, haben wir hier zusammengestellt. Ob wir mit dieser Prognose Recht behalten werden, wird sich natürlich erst in einigen Jahrzehnten herausstellen …

## Arturia PolyBrute 12: Ausdrucksstärkster Analogsynthesizer aller Zeiten?

Angesichts der vielen bemerkenswerten Hardware-Synthesizer, für die Arturia heute bekannt ist, könnte man glatt vergessen, dass der französische Hersteller ursprünglich eine reine Software-Firma war. In den letzten gut zehn Jahren hat sich das gründlich geändert und Arturia hat mittlerweile mehr als einen Hardware-Synthesizer im Programm, der das Zeug zum Klassiker hat. Auf den **MiniFreak**am unteren Ende der Preisspanne trifft das meiner Ansicht nach durchaus auch zu, genauso wie auf den**MiniBrute**.

Der **PolyBrute 12**steht jedoch noch einmal auf einer ganz anderen Stufe. Das liegt in erster Linie an der unglaublich ausdrucksstark spielbaren**FullTouch-Tastatur**. Sie verleiht dem Synthesizer eine ganz neue Ebene der Expressivität, die man so bei kaum einem anderen Instrument findet – schon gar nicht bei einem Analogsynthesizer. Aber auch klanglich hat der PolyBrute 12 mit seinen Brute-Oszillatoren, den dualen Filtern und der umfangreichen Modulationsmatrix einiges zu bieten.

Arturia PolyBrute 12 · Quelle: Arturia

In unserem **[Angecheckt](https://www.gearnews.de/arturia-polybrute-12-test/)** schreibt mein Kollege Rob Puricelli: „Der Arturia PolyBrute 12 ist eine Zäsur. Eine Linie im Sand, könnte man sagen. […] Er ist ein Musikinstrument im wahrsten Sinn des Wortes.” Das dürfte reichen, um in ein paar Jahrzehnten als Meilenstein der Synthesizer-Geschichte und als Synthesizer-Klassiker zu gelten. Der Synthesizer ist bei [Thomann](https://www.thomann.de/de/arturia_polybrute_12.htm?offid=1&affid=84)* erhältlich.

## Moog Mother-Serie: Semi-modular für alle

Als Moog im Jahr 2015 den **[Mother-32](https://www.gearnews.de/news-moog-mother-32-moog-sound-fuers-eurorack/)**herausbrachte, betrat der Hersteller Neuland. Etwas Vergleichbares gab es damals nicht. Der**semi-modulare**und damals vergleichsweise günstige**Analogsynthesizer**war einfach zu bedienen, brachte seinen eigenen**Sequencer** mit und lieferte schon ohne Patch-Verbindungen einen satten Sound. Zugleich war er aber auch die perfekte „Einstiegsdroge” in die modulare Welt. Für unzählige Synthesizer-Fans wurde der Mother-32 zum Beginn einer modularen Leidenschaft. Praktisch, dass man ihn auf Wunsch direkt ins Eurorack einbauen kann!

Moog Sound Studio mit Mother-32, DFAM und Subharmonicon · Quelle: Moog

Später ergänzte Moog die Serie um den **[DFAM](https://www.gearnews.de/moog-dfam-limitierte-submutter-fuer-drums/)**, das eigenwillige**[Subharmonicon](https://www.gearnews.de/moog-subharmonicon-subharmonic-synthesizer/)**und schließlich den**[Labyrinth](https://www.gearnews.de/moog-labyrinth/)**und**[Spectravox](https://www.gearnews.de/moog-spectravox/)**. Im Team bilden die Synthesizer ein semi-modulares Klanglabor, das seinesgleichen sucht. Folglich gab es verschiedene Kombinationen der Synthesizer zeitweise auch als komplettes**[Moog Sound Studio](https://www.gearnews.de/moog-sound-studio-mother-32-dfam-subharmonicon/)** zu kaufen.

Continuing their series on how our brains find the right paths, Aatish Bhatia and Arkarup Banerjee show the learning process through “sparks” that stand in as simplified versions of brains [moving through a space of possible brains](https://aatishb.com/myriad/how-brains-learn/).

> It’s worth taking a moment to appreciate how surprising this is — given enough tries, the same learning process turned every novice into an expert light seeker.
> Of the myriad possible arrangements of this spark’s brain, only a tiny fraction generate the behavior that we want. There are far more ways to fail than to succeed.
> And yet, you’ve just witnessed a small miracle. The spark navigated this labyrinth of dead ends and rewired its brain to find the light, guided by nothing but reward and punishment.

items.body: IntroductionReduced executive functioning (EF) - including inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, and working memory - has been frequently observed among adolescents and young adults living with HIV (AYALH), despite antiretroviral therapy (ART). These deficits may reflect HIV-associated alterations in brain structure and function. This review aimed to synthesize the available evidence of this relationship.MethodsFollowing the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, we searched PsycINFO, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases for relevant studies reporting EF outcomes and neural correlates (structural or functional).ResultsTwenty studies met the inclusion criteria. Significantly lower brain volumes and cortical thickness, lower fractional anisotropy, higher mean diffusivity, higher cerebral blood flow, and altered cerebral metabolites were observed among AYALH relative to matched controls. EF problems, particularly in working memory, were frequently reported. Overall, the observed neural alterations correlated with decreased EF among AYALH.ConclusionDespite ART use, HIV-associated neural alterations and executive function deficits still occur or persist among adolescents and young adults living with HIV. Preliminary evidence suggests that distinct HIV-associated neural alterations may be associated with EF problems in AYALH. Neuroimaging may offer insights into these cognitive difficulties, although more longitudinal and multimodal studies are needed.Systematic Review RegistrationThis review is registered in PROSPERO (https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/), registration number: CRD42025639283.

items.body:
When [Ableton](https://musictech.com/brands/ableton)’s Push 3 hit the market in 2023, it was framed as [a generational piece of kit](https://musictech.com/features/interviews/ableton-push-3-timeless-instrument-new-generation/). Not only did it ‘push’ the series into a new realm, able to operate as a totally standalone controller rather than a loyal [Ableton Live](https://musictech.com/tag/ableton-live) companion, but the Push’s third iteration also tightened things up. With a refined workflow, new modes like Autowarping, and a fresh grid of 64 expressive MPE pads, it was Ableton mastering the controller formula – and [it’s currently available for $360 off at Sweetwater](https://sweetwater.sjv.io/N9kLeN).

[deals ids=”42cf3ac6-66c1-439e-bd7d-86825d6cc3ba”]

To this day, the [controller](https://musictech.com/tag/controllers) continues to hold its own. And that’s because, alongside all the perks, Ableton’s design allows for the Push 3 to grow with you; the upgradable, modular system is built to last. Whether it’s a battery upgrade or processing update, Push 3 has the potential to keep up with even the freshest tech.

With that in mind, the Push 3 was never ‘just for Christmas’ – it’s a device you can invest in, knowing it would serve you well for years to come. That’s what makes Sweetwater’s current Black Friday even sweeter; for $1,439, you’ll get a quality controller that is an absolute powerhouse.

While the drop to $1,439 from $1,799 is already pretty nice, the deal only gets sweeter the more you consider it. Because it doesn’t just bag you a controller, but the ability to mix and edit without the need for Ableton Live. It’s a built-in audio/MIDI interface, making it a handy central hub for your entire rig.

However, if you know you’re someone who always plans to hook their controller up to their computer, there is also a deal on the Push 3 without a built-in processor. [The Push 3 Control Surface](https://www.sweetwater.com/store/detail/Push3--ableton-push-3) is exactly that, and it’s available at just $799, a $200 from its usual cost of $999. But, to reiterate, this option does require you to hook it up to a computer running Ableton Live.

**For more information, head to [Sweetwater](https://sweetwater.sjv.io/N9kLeN). If you’re interested in finding any other good deals, feel free to check out our full guide to[Black Friday](https://musictech.com/news/gear/best-black-friday-music-tech-deals/).**

items.body:
Auch in diesem Schuljahr veranstaltet die Föderation der Deutsch-Französischen Häuser den deutsch-französischen Geschichtswettbewerb EUSTORY-France. Der diesjährige Wettbewerb befasst sich mit dem Thema: « Klima- und Umweltschutz schreibt Geschichte. Engagement und Protest in Deutschland und Frankreich ». Er lädt Schüler*innen der 8. Klasse bis zum Abitur in Deutschland und Frankreich (4e bis zur Terminale) ein, sich mit dem vorgegebenen Thema auseinanderzusetzen und einen Beitrag zu verfassen – in Einzel- oder Gruppenarbeit oder idealerweise im deutsch-französischen Tandem.

**Klima- und Umweltschutz schreibt Geschichte. Engagement und Protest in Deutschland und Frankreich**

Menschen haben seit jeher ihre Umwelt beeinflusst. Aber beginnend mit der Industrialisierung im 18. Jh. ist das Ausmaß dieses Eingriffs ein anderes geworden: Maschinen, Fabriken und große Städte verändern nicht nur das Leben der Menschen – sondern auch die Natur. Die Folgen werden immer mehr spürbar. Vereinzelt werden Menschen laut, die fordern, dass sich etwas ändern muss. Sie machen auf Missstände aufmerksam, schließen sich mit Anderen zusammen, protestieren oder rütteln mit spektakulären Aktionen wach und schaffen es, Veränderungen herbeizuführen.

**Der Wettbewerb möchte es genauer wissen:**

Von ganz frühen Naturschutzinitiativen über erste Anti-Atomkraft-Proteste der 1970er Jahre und globale Klimadebatten seit den 1980er Jahren bis heute: Was hat Menschen in Deutschland und Frankreich zum Handeln gebracht? Was waren ihre Ängste und Hoffnungen? Welche Erzählungen und Konflikte prägten die Debatten innerhalb und außerhalb der Bewegungen? Und wer bestimmte mit – Menschen aus der Wissenschaft, der Politik oder der Zivilgesellschaft?

Welche Formen wählten sie für ihr Engagement? Was waren ihre Erfolge und Niederlagen? Wie ist es ihnen gelungen, in unseren Gesellschaften etwas zu verändern? Und wie kann aus der Idee Einzelner eine politische Entscheidung werden?

Der Wettbewerb lädt dazu ein, die Suche vor der Haustür zu beginnen, lokale Geschichte zu erforschen und in einen breiter gefassten, deutsch-französischen und europäischen Kontext zu setzen. Welche Rolle spielte internationale Vernetzung? Welche Gemeinsamkeiten und/oder Unterschiede gab es zwischen den deutschen und französischen Bewegungen?

Und genauso wichtig: Welche Menschen und Ereignisse aus der Vergangenheit machen heute Mut? Was lässt uns lernen für unsere Zukunft – und die der kommenden Generationen? Denn die Geschichte des Klima- und Umweltschutzes erzählt von Verantwortung, Engagement und Protest – und sie ist noch nicht zu Ende geschrieben.

Die besten Beiträge werden mit Preisen ausgezeichnet, die im Juli 2027 im Rahmen einer offiziellen Preisverleihung überreicht werden.

[Weitere Infos & Anmeldung](https://eustory.fr)

*Eine Meldung der EUSTORY-France.*

items.body:
> Between 1970 and 1990 the U.S. legal services industry underwent a dramatic demand shift. Its employment share more than doubled and the relative wages of lawyers rose by 60%, in contrast to stability before and after. We attribute this shift to three related changes in the legal environment: a wave of new legislation and regulation broadened the scope of the law, left its application uncertain, and enlisted private lawyers to enforce it through fee-shifting. Using over a century of data, we show that lawyers’ employment and compensation track all three changes. Event studies link specific statutes to increased litigation and demand for the affected fields of law. Other explanations, including lawyer quality, industrial composition, and technology, do not account for the demand shift. We estimate that legislative uncertainty accounts for roughly 13% of the demand shift—a cost of about $23 billion in 2024 alone.

That is from [a new paper](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5acd55db36099bfff90bf5d6/t/6ab43b507bff7c595f110ab3/1790196560274/ReshefSlattery_Lawyers_Sept2026.pdf) by Ariell Resheff and Cailin Slattery. Via [Krzysztof Tyszka-Drozdowski](https://tyszka-drozdowski.com/).

items.body:
On a foggy September morning in 1877, Eugene Victor Debs adjusted his suit collar and set out for the Indiana State House. Just shy of twenty-two years old, he’d been a member of his labor union, the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen, for barely two and a half years. But today he would deliver the opening address to its national convention.

Horse-drawn wagons and carriages rolled through the downtown streets of Indianapolis, clacking on the cobblestones and kicking up gravel as paved stretches came to an end. Lavishly ornamented cast-iron buildings mingled with simple brick structures; steam whistles sounded from the railroad tracks bound for the teeming Union Depot, the first in the country to bring all train traffic to a central hub. City leaders were thinking longterm here. Meatpacking was the city’s other big industry, Kingan and Company’s mammoth plant one of the largest in the world, its state-of-the-art chilling system allowing year-round production in these days before refrigeration.

Theirs was grimy, dangerous work.

Indianapolis wasn’t Chicago or St. Louis, Midwestern metropolises with populations in the hundreds of thousands, but its 75,000 inhabitants painted a smaller-scale picture of a rapidly industrializing America. With all the corresponding possibilities and cruelties. The boom-and-bust of capitalism had gone bust four years before in the so-called Panic of 1873, an economic disaster nearly as severe as the Great Depression of the 1930s—and joblessness persisted in Indianapolis, as elsewhere. Workers terrified of being laid off grudgingly accepted wage cuts. Politicians responded to calls for a public jobs program with creative new punishments instead: fines for begging, a proposed workhouse “where all persons incapable of paying fines” would be forced to smash stones to pave more city streets.

Soon, Gene Debs would have seen the Indiana State House come into view. A white wooden fence edged the tree-lined lawn—the trunks like matchsticks, branches draped with green leaves holding on despite the imminent change in seasons. The dome of the state capitol rose above, a grand if crumbling structure of blue limestone and gray stuccoed columns patterned on the Greek Parthenon. Debs—amiable and outgoing, a bit over six feet tall, with a slim but solid build—entered the capitol and mounted the stairs to the House of Representatives’ chamber on the upper floor, which the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen was borrowing for the convention. He greeted his fellow delegates, who had exchanged their soot-stained work clothes for suits and ties.

Theirs was grimy, dangerous work. Firemen shoveled the coal that powered steam engines into the locomotive’s firebox, which was prone to explosion. Every month the firemen’s magazine carried grim news of widowed wives, orphaned children, maimed railroaders. Train derailments and collisions were ubiquitous. Railroad workers made up the bulk of workplace injuries in Gilded Age America: by one count 56 percent of the broken ribs, 50 percent of broken arms, 41 percent of broken legs, 71 percent of severed arms, and all of the amputated legs.

Nearly one in four trainmen could expect to die on the job if he worked for thirty years; only coal mining was as lethal. The work was well paid by the standards of the day, with veteran engineers often able to own their own home, but shifts were long and irregular, running anywhere from twelve to twenty-four hours, or longer. “It is no uncommon thing,” one railroader said, “for an engineer to go for nearly a week without sleep except in snatches on the road or waiting on a branch or engine house.” Workers lived close to the railyards, knowing that at a moment’s notice they could be gone for days or weeks. The imperatives of their employers, rather than their own individual wants or collective needs, governed workers’ lives.

Not that Debs begrudged the railroad companies. If the work was too dangerous or too demanding, the hours too long or the bosses too harsh, it was up to railroad workers to prove themselves worthy of more respect. If they could do so—if they could renounce strikes and hard-drinking and rebelliousness, if they could live out the brotherhood’s motto of “benevo-lence, sobriety, industry”—then the companies would treat them with the dignity they deserved and pay them a decent wage. He was sure of it.

The story of Eugene V. Debs’s life is the story of one man’s radicalization—and of the country he helped radicalize in turn.

That summer, as far as Debs was concerned, rail workers had done the opposite.

Exhausted by four dragging years of economic depression, railroaders had struck by the tens of thousands, from the East Coast to the Corn Belt, inspiring hundreds of thousands of other workers to join them on strike. It was the first walkout of its size in United States history. The government treated it as an insurrection. President Rutherford B. Hayes sent in federal troops and militias, who shot down protesters, which triggered violence and widespread destruction of railroad property—torched locomotives, smoldering roundhouses, train tracks turned into twisted hulks of metal. The question at the heart of the Great Upheaval, as it came to be called, was whether the nation’s industrial development would benefit the workers who stoked the engines and ran the cotton looms and mined the coal, or whether it would anoint a new class of economic barons who’d monopolize the country’s wealth and power. “It is wrong to call this a strike,” one newspaper announced. “It is a labor revolution.”

And that’s exactly what Eugene Debs—a fresh-faced twenty-one years old, idealistic and respectable—did not want. After all, those same railroad companies that workers struck against had granted the brotherhood’s delegates free transport to their national convention. What better sign of the rail lines’ goodwill? What stronger proof of the benefits of currying favor with employers?

…

items.body:
## Photographer Shares the Emotional Story Behind an Elephant Carrying Its Stillborn Calf [Interview]

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/federico-veronesi-wildlife-photography/)

“The Aftermath”

Wildlife photographer [Federico Veronesi](https://federicoveronesi.com/) encountered the shot of a lifetime in Damaraland, Namibia. In September 2025, he witnessed a desert elephant carrying its stillborn calf. What resulted was an arresting black-and-white image that is beautifully composed but ultimately full of grief. The close-up portrait shows the mother with her deceased calf between her tusk and trunk, as if she is unable to let her baby go. The emotional image, titled *The Aftermath*, was recognized in the prestigious [Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 competition](https://mymodernmet.com/natural-history-museum-wildlife-photographer-of-the-year-2026/), with Veronesi earning the title of Overall Winner and the Behavior Mammals category winner.

Veronesi was tracking elephants when he noticed an unusual pattern of drag marks in the sand of a dry riverbed. He understood why when he saw the mother and child. “The calf’s body rose up and in this particular frame, it almost looks like the calf is still alive, playing with its mother or trying to cling to her mother’s trunk,” he recalls to My Modern Met. “I feel that the ambiguity of the image, and how it can be read in many ways make it stand out from the other images I took, where the calf is clearly hanging lifeless from the mother’s tusk.”

The photographer initially felt conflicted about capturing the scene. “After taking the first few images, I felt like I was violating the elephant’s intimate moment, her grief, I was almost ashamed and thought that I shouldn’t take these photographs,” he shares. But ultimately, Veronesi found it important to highlight the complexity of these creatures. Elephants have been observed engaging in behaviors around death, including vocalizing, guarding the deceased, and carrying the dead, as pictured. By photographing this painful moment, Veronesi shows us that wildlife and humans aren’t as far apart as we may think.

We spoke with Veronesi about capturing the poignant shot, his philosophy about photographing wildlife, and more. Scroll down for My Modern Met’s exclusive interview.

**What is your photography background, and how did you begin photographing wildlife?**

Photography was part of my life since an early age as I grew up in a family of keen nature photographers. Every travel or outing was always centered on photographing nature, birds and wildlife in particular. I therefore learned photography almost naturally. I began photographing wildlife with my Polaroid on my first trip to Africa when I was 6 years old or to the local zoos and safari parks. During my teenage years I upgraded to a reflex camera and slides, and that’s what I used for my first years in Kenya after I moved there in 2002 to follow my dream of living among wildlife and photographing it full time.

**Set up the scene for your image The Aftermath, which shows an elephant carrying a dead calf. How did you come across this?**

I was in Damaraland, northwestern Namibia, with the specific aim to photograph desert-adapted elephants and other wildlife living in this particularly dry but stunning ecosystem. Elephants are frequently found along the dry riverbeds that traverse this landscape, as that’s where they find some trees and vegetation that they can feed on. I had seen a family of elephants the previous evening, so that morning I returned to the place where I left them to pick up their tracks and hopefully find them again. As I followed the tracks, I noticed an unusual dragging mark on the ground, which I wasn’t immediately able to interpret. Shortly after I finally came across the elephants feeding on the river banks. Out of the group, a female appeared carrying a dead calf by wedging the calf’s leg between her trunk and tusk.

**How did the final image emerge? Did you realize the photograph’s importance when you snapped it?**

As the scene appeared in front of me, I grabbed my 400mm telephoto lens and framed the images, I went for a vertical crop as she was coming towards me and she filled the frame nicely. As she came forward, another elephant was following her, so she abruptly turned away. The calf’s body rose up and in this particular frame, it almost looks like the calf is still alive, playing with its mother or trying to cling to her mother’s trunk. I feel that the ambiguity of the image, and how it can be read in many ways make it stand out from the other images I took, where the calf is clearly hanging lifeless from the mother’s tusk. After taking the first few images I felt like I was violating the elephant’s intimate moment, her grief, I was almost ashamed and thought that I shouldn’t take these photographs. However, as I reflected on the event, I realized how important it was for me to tell the story, to offer people an open window into the soul of the elephant, into her feelings, into her memories, hopefully to make people understand the complexity of the animals’ emotions and sensibility. That’s why I also chose black and white, to expose these emotions without any possible distraction.

**What is your philosophy when photographing wildlife? **

When I am photographing wildlife, I am always looking for images where I can reveal how similar we are to them on an emotional level, and to establish a connection on the emotional level. I like to try to tell their story, and our story through them somehow. I strive to make images where people can see themselves in the animals. All of this while never disturbing the animals, never altering their behavior, and never manipulating my images digitally.

**What can it tell us about our own humanity?**

items.body:
Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of [Cappadocia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cappadocia), a millennia-old tradition continues. Here in Central Anatolia, Turkey, horses have been a part of daily life, civic programs, and military campaigns since prehistory. In *[The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse](https://hemeria.com/en-us/products/the-untold-story-of-the-yilki-horses)*, photographer [Nur Tucker](https://nurtucker.com/) captures a portrait of the region’s living heritage.

Published by Hemeria, the title delves into the beauty and tenacity of the semi-wild horses while also highlighting the lifestyles of those who herd them through rugged landscapes. Tucker, who is a British-Turkish photographer based in the U.K., has long been drawn to the vigor and elegance of horses, and the [yilki breed](https://www.yilkiatlari.org.tr/en/history.html) that populates Anatolia have a particularly resonant history.

“Yilki” comes from the Turkish verb *yılmak*, which means “to flee” or “to be set loose.” The name “has come to describe the condition of these herds that live between liberation and loss, between domestic heritage and wild abandon,” says a statement.

In a place where horses have been bred for agriculture, transportation, battle, and more for thousands of years, their role forever changed within just the past century due to mechanization and industrialization. With motorized tractors, trucks, and cars to work the fields and provide transportation, horses essentially became redundant. Released to fend for themselves, they survived harsh winters, bred on their own, and grew into sizable herds. In *The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse,* Tucker composes a love letter to these striking animals, celebrating their resilience through more than 100 images.

The book is available for purchase directly from [Hemeria](https://hemeria.com/en-us/products/the-untold-story-of-the-yilki-horses), and it’s slated for worldwide release next October. See more on Tucker’s [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/nurtuckerphotography/?hl=en).

Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a [Colossal Member](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/members) today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article [Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/11/the-untold-story-of-the-yilki-horse-nur-tucker-book/) appeared first on [Colossal](https://www.thisiscolossal.com).

items.title: Avoiding disempowerment through protectionism?

items.body:
Recently many people are debating whether AI will lead to our disempowerment. One simple example is that we might use AI to pursue or solve various intellectual tasks for us, rather than doing it ourselves.

So say there are twenty important math problems, and we let the AIs (with some human guidance) take a crack at them. Say the AIs solve seventeen of those problems, the humans one, and two remain unsolved.

Alternately, say we ban or limit AIs, and over a longer period of time the humans solve three of those problems. The rest go unsolved.

Arguably in the latter situation the humans are exercising more agency and, as unaided humans, achieving greater things. But in the former situation there is more discovery, possibly more usefulness, and the marginal impact of total human effort (including building the AIs) is far greater.

Which scenario involves greater “disempowerment”? I do not view the concept of disempowerment as entirely well defined, but it seems to my virgin eyes that the humans are more “disempowered” in the latter case, where only three of the problems get solved.

And take those two extra problems that get solved (eventually) by humans. Should we feel empowered if we achieve two theorem proofs due to what you might call protectionism, or how about labeling it “DEI for humans”?

Say I was working on a difficult economics problem, and I learned that an unpublished manuscript from China had solved the problem. But no one else knows about the manuscript, except for me that is. I could announce the manuscript and give it full credit. Or I could ignore the manuscript and claim the credit, and the “empowerment,” for myself. Should I feel so satisfied by that latter approach?

Or let’s say that Chinese manuscript does not exist, but I could help to create it by a well-targeted EV grant. I decline to give the grant so I can do the work myself and feel “empowered.” Am I really so empowered? Or is it a kind of phony triumph, because someone or something else could have done it better.

(One thing I have always liked about being an academic economist, or for that matter an internet writer, is knowing that I am competing against the entire world. In the U.S. academic job market there has been de facto open borders for a long time, since university employers usually will get visas for their hires, and do not shy away from doing that, even today.)

As for AI, should I feel so good and empowered if I achieve things only by deliberately holding the machines back? Or, in that scenario, am I just a loser who deliberately shuns competition?

Here is [one relevant tweet](https://x.com/centralunplan/status/2123301123901804658?a=XXtuj-4hIL366IlB0QM&s=61).

In general, I am not persuaded by the notion of empowering humans by bathing the world in protectionism and “DEI for humans.” I feel humans will be empowered best by finding their true marginally most important contributions and making those. Whether or not that involves doing the exact same things we are contributing at today.
