items.feedText:
Federico Viticci dove in and figured out how the whole system, which routes commands back through the Claude app, works, and came to this conclusion:

If I were Apple, I’d be concerned. Effectively, Anthropic shipped an app creation playground that only requires basic prompts to put together something that works. They did so by entirely bypassing the App Store or Apple’s notarization system for apps distributed outside the App Store, and by creating their own lock-in system around Claude’s identity and capabili…
items.body:
Anthropic now offers a way to [convert Claude artifacts into things that look a lot like native Mac (and Windows) apps](https://claude.com/resources/articles/install-as-app). Federico Viticci dove in and figured out how the whole system, which routes commands back through the Claude app, works, and [came to this conclusion](https://www.macstories.net/stories/a-closer-look-at-claudes-mac-apps/):

> If I were Apple, I’d be concerned. Effectively, Anthropic shipped an app creation playground that only requires basic prompts to put together something that works. They did so by entirely bypassing the App Store or Apple’s notarization system for apps distributed outside the App Store, and by creating their own lock-in system around Claude’s identity and capabilities instead.

It’s been [crystal clear for a while now](https://sixcolors.com/post/2026/06/road-to-wwdc-2026-whats-a-developer/) that Apple needs a simplified set of app building tools that don’t look like Xcode. This area is moving fast—even faster than I thought—and regular people are now able to [develop their own custom apps](https://www.theincomparable.com/doubleender/) with ease.

Anthropic’s solution is interesting, but it’s also full of limitations and clever hacks. That’s not the issue, though. The issue is that this stuff is going to keep getting better and Apple needs to get in the game as soon as possible.

[Go to the linked site](https://www.macstories.net/stories/a-closer-look-at-claudes-mac-apps/).

[Read on Six Colors](https://sixcolors.com/link/2026/11/claude-now-lets-you-vibe-code-html-mac-apps/).

items.body:
For the first time ever, a foreign astronaut has set foot inside China's Tiangong space station.

That pioneer is Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, who arrived at [Tiangong](https://www.space.com/tiangong-space-station) aboard the [Shenzhou-24](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/human-spaceflight/china-rolls-out-rocket-for-launch-of-1st-international-astronaut-to-tiangong-space-station-video) spacecraft early this morning (Nov. 25).

"The Chinese space station is always something to look forward to!" the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) wrote in [an update today](https://www.cmse.gov.cn/xwzx/202611/t20261125_57903.html) (in Mandarin; translation by Google). "China's 'Tiangong' welcomes partners from all over the world to visit!"

Ali, a former pilot in Pakistan's armed forces, is a payload specialist on Shenzhou-24. He found his way onto the mission thanks to a space-cooperation agreement that China signed with Pakistan in Islamabad [in February 2025](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/human-spaceflight/china-and-pakistan-agree-to-fly-1st-foreign-astronaut-to-chinese-space-station).

Ali and his two Shenzhou-24 crewmates — commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi — enjoyed a short and smooth ride to their orbital destination. They [lifted off](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/human-spaceflight/china-shenzhou-24-first-international-astronaut-launch-tiangong-space-station) atop a Long March 2F rocket on Tuesday (Nov. 24) at 7:18 p.m. EST (0018 GMT on Nov. 25) and reached Tiangong a little over six hours later.

Tang and Wu will live aboard the outpost for the usual six-month stint. Ali, however, will come home in just a week, hitching a ride with two of the three Shenzhou-23 astronauts, who [arrived at Tiangong in May](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/human-spaceflight/china-shenzhou-23-astronaut-launch-tiangong-space-station).

Ali will be busy during his short space stay, conducting a set of joint Chinese-Pakistani experiments.

"Four collaborative projects in biotechnology and materials are planned, with Ali also scheduled to conduct an in-orbit experiment involving photosynthetic cyanobacteria," The Times of India [wrote today](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/science/pak-astronaut-ali-reaches-chinas-tiangong-station/articleshow/136152904.cms).

The third Shenzhou-23 crewmate, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain on the station until Shenzhou-24 comes home. Zhu will therefore set a Chinese record, becoming the first astronaut from his country to live in [low Earth orbit](https://www.space.com/low-earth-orbit) for a full year.

Astronauts from the Soviet Union/Russia and the United States have already blazed this long-duration trail. The global record for longest continuous space stay is 437 days, set by cosmonaut Valeri Polyakov aboard the [Mir space station](https://www.space.com/31999-mir-space-station-30th-anniversary.html) from January 1994 to March 1995.

Another look at the Shenzhou-23 and Shenzhou-24 astronauts aboard Tiangong on Nov. 25, 2026. (Image credit: CMSA)

Ali is not the first person from Pakistan ever to reach space, by the way. That distinction belongs to adventurer Namira Salim, who [traveled to suborbital space](https://www.space.com/virgin-galactic-first-pakistani-space-galactic04) on a tourism flight with [Virgin Galactic](https://www.space.com/18993-virgin-galactic.html) in October 2023.

Shenzhou-24 is the 12th crewed mission to Tiangong, a three-module, T-shaped outpost that China finished assembling in late 2022. Well, "finished" might not be the right term; China [plans to expand Tiangong](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/china-plans-to-double-the-size-of-its-tiangong-space-station-while-the-iss-nears-its-end), which is currently about 20% as massive as the [International Space Station](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/missions/international-space-station).

In [an announcement on Wednesday](https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-427572A1.pdf), the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned [company's "Starmind" initiative](https://www.spacex.com/spacexsi/starmind). With [several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/845453/space-data-centers-astronomers), including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency has granted for a full "constellation" of AI satellites.

The FCC also deferred SpaceX's request to dispose of satellites located above 600km in [space "graveyard" orbits](https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/news/graveyard-orbits-and-the-satellite-afterlife), rather than …

items.body:
After four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the [Ladybird](https://ladybird.org/) project released its first [downloadable alpha](https://ladybird.org/download/) on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux. Previously, curious users had to compile the browser themselves from its source. Now it's an installable package with automatic updating.

Ladybird is most notable for what it isn't: another browser fork. Where Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera all run on Google's Blink engine, and Firefox depends on Gecko, Ladybird's rendering engine and its [LibJS JavaScript engine](https://ladybirdbrowser.github.io/libjs-website/) were written from scratch. "The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork," project lead Andreas Kling wrote in Monday's announcement. "The browser around it is modest, but functional."

## A fourth engine

Nearly the entire modern web currently runs on three browser engines. There's [WebKit](https://webkit.org/) (Safari), [Gecko](https://firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org/overview/gecko.html) (Firefox), and the biggest of them all, [Blink](https://www.chromium.org/blink/) (Chromium). Those limited options mean that web developers often end up optimizing sites for Chromium specifically, since that's where the majority of traffic is, and as a result, the whole web platform tends to follow suit toward whatever the dominant engine supports.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/11/ladybirds-new-alpha-shows-theres-life-beyond-chromium/)

# Raumsonde „Hera“ erreicht Asteroiden Dimorphos - Wissen - SZ.de

Die Raumsonde „Hera“ ist aktuell etwa 30 Kilometer von den Asteroiden Didymos und Dimorphos entfernt. Esa 2022 ließ die Nasa eine Sonde auf den Asteroiden Dimorphos prallen, um ihn aus seiner Bahn zu lenken. Nun ist eine Sonde der Esa eingetroffen. Was die Bilder zeigen.

Von Theresa Palm

E r sei beim Blick auf die ersten Bilder zusammengezuckt, erzählt Patrick Michel. Der leitende Wissenschaftler der Hera-Mission bei der Esa forscht am französischen Observatoire de la Côte d’Azur. Und er sagt: Man habe sofort den Effekt des Einschlags vor vier Jahren sehen können.

items.body:
# Spuren des Einschlags: Hera entdeckt riesigen Krater auf Dimorphos - Spektrum der Wissenschaft

## Spuren des Einschlags: Hera entdeckt riesigen Krater auf Dimorphos

Startseite Astronomie Aktuelle Seite: Spuren des Einschlags: Hera entdeckt riesigen Krater auf Dimorphos © ESA / Hera reveals stadium-sized asteroid crater from spacecraft impact (Ausschnitt) Durch den gezielten Beschuss mit der NASA-Raumsonde DART am 26. September 2026 entstand ein im Vergleich zum 151 Meter großen Asteroiden Dimorphos (kleineres Objekt oben links) riesiger Krater, der etwa ein Drittel bis zur Hälfte der getroffenen Hemisphäre einnimmt. Dadurch wurden die Form und die Bahn des Himmelskörpers beträchtlich verändert. Vor etwas mehr als vier Jahren, am 26. September 2022, schlug die NASA-Raumsonde DART , der Double Asteroid Redirection Test, gezielt mit rund sechs Kilometern pro Sekunde wie ein Projektil auf Dimorphos ein. Dieser ist der kleinere Begleiter des Asteroiden Didymos; gemeinsam bilden sie ein gravitativ gebundenes System. Beim Impakt wurden große Mengen an Felsbrocken und Staub aus dem nur 151 Meter großen Asteroidenmond herausgeschleudert. Sie bildeten einen Schweif, der auch von der Erde aus verfolgt werden konnte. Am Abend des 25. November 2026 stellte die Europäische Raumfahrtagentur ESA erstmals Bilder vor, welche die Folgen des Einschlags der rund eine halbe Tonne schweren Sonde zeigen. Auf Dimorphos ist ein im Verhältnis zum Himmelskörper riesiger Einschlagkrater entstanden, der rund ein Drittel bis zur Hälfte der getroffenen Hemisphäre einnimmt (siehe »Dimorphos vor und nach dem Treffer von DART«). Die ESA vergleicht ihn mit der Größe eines Stadions. © NASA/Johns Hopkins APL (links); ESA (rechts) / Hera reveals stadium-sized asteroid crater from spacecraft impact (Ausschnitt) Dimorphos vor und nach dem Treffer von DART | Mehr als vier Jahre liegen zwischen dem Bild der NASA-Raumsonde DART (links) vom 26. September 2022 und dem Bild der europäischen Sonde Hera von Mitte November 2026 (rechts). Auf dem Mond Dimorphos (kleineres Objekt links vom Hauptkörper Didymos) entstand durch den gezielten Einschlag der Raumsonde DART ein im Verhältnis zum 151 Meter großen Dimorphos riesiger Krater, der die Form des Himmelskörpers drastisch veränderte. In der Mitte des Kraters lässt sich auch eine zigarrenförmige Zentralerhebung erkennen. Vor den Aufnahmen der Raumsonde Hera war unklar , welche Folgen der Einschlag von DART auf Dimorphos hatte. Die Bandbreite der Vermutungen erstreckte sich von kaum sichtbar bis zu einem riesigen Loch, wobei Letzteres eindrucksvoll bestätigt wurde. Beim Aufprall wurde DART innerhalb von Sekundenbruchteilen vollständig zerstört. Lediglich eine zuvor ausgesetzte Subsonde von der Größe eines Schuhkartons lieferte Aufnahmen des Einschlags, allerdings aus einer Perspektive, von der aus die Einschlagnarbe nicht sichtbar war. Weite Aufnahmen von Hera zeigen zudem, dass die Region um den Doppelasteroiden Didymos/Dimorphos für Raumsonden sehr gefährlich ist, denn Hunderte von Felsbrocken von bis zu mehreren Metern Durchmesser treiben sich im Umfeld der beiden Himmelskörper herum (siehe »Gefährlicher Schwarm«). Sie wurden beim Einschlag von DART nicht ausreichend beschleunigt, um das schwache Schwerefeld von Didymos zu verlassen. Sie zeigen sich auf langbelichteten Aufnahmen. Somit hat Didymos mittlerweile nicht nur einen, sondern Hunderte von Monden. © ESA / Hera reveals stadium-sized asteroid crater from spacecraft impact (Ausschnitt) Gefährlicher Schwarm | Hunderte Felsbrocken unterschiedlicher Größe ziehen durch das Didymos/Dimorphos-System. Ihre Bewegungen sind in dieser zusammengesetzten Aufnahme als punktförmige Spuren zu erkennen. Das Bild vereint elf Langzeitbelichtungen, die mit der Hyperscout-H-Kamera am 6. November aus einer Entfernung von etwa 29,9 Kilometern aufgenommen wurden. Didymos und Dimorphos wurden aus der Darstellung herausgerechnet (große schwarze Flecken in der Bildmitte), damit die umliegenden Gesteinsbrocken besser zur Geltung kommen.

items.title: A Closer Look at Claude’s Mac “Apps”
items.subtitle: Yesterday, Anthropic announced a major new feature for artifacts, now available in beta for Mac and Windows: the ability for users to turn artifact…
items.feedText: Yesterday, Anthropic announced a major new feature for artifacts, now available in beta for Mac and Windows: the ability for users to turn artifacts into “apps” they can install on their computers. From the [company’s blog](https://claude.com/resources/articles/install-as-app): > Starting today, you can use Claude artifacts to create, run, and share desktop apps. The “Install as app” feature is rolling out in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows. > When an artifact is installed as a Mac or Windows app, it gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. You can share it with others, and it needs your permission before it can interact with your computer. You choose how much to allow.
items.body:
Yesterday, Anthropic announced a major new feature for artifacts, now available in beta for Mac and Windows: the ability for users to turn artifacts into “apps” they can install on their computers. From the [company’s blog](https://claude.com/resources/articles/install-as-app):

> Starting today, you can use Claude artifacts to create, run, and share desktop apps. The “Install as app” feature is rolling out in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows.
> When an artifact is installed as a Mac or Windows app, it gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. You can share it with others, and it needs your permission before it can interact with your computer. You choose how much to allow.
> Each app can use Claude and your connectors, and it updates automatically when the underlying artifact is edited. This simplifies the process for building and maintaining apps for both knowledge workers and developers. Requests the app makes to Claude count toward your plan’s usage limits.

If you’re an [AppStories](https://www.macstories.net/show/appstories) listener, you know that I’ve long thought it was only a matter of time until one of the big labs figured out how to turn their models’ frontier coding capabilities into a means to disrupt the App Store. This move feels like Anthropic’s first step in that direction.

Before I get into the technical details, let me say this upfront: if I were Apple, I’d be *very* concerned that Anthropic is now shipping a nicely packaged system for users to make whatever app they want and turn Apple’s ecosystem into **Claude’s ecosystem** of tools and mods on their computers.

Now, the way Anthropic made this happen can be debated, but I think the system is based on some clever engineering and savvy lock-in strategy. First, for these apps to work, you need the main Claude app to be installed and logged in with your account. These apps require the main Claude process to be running because every action they perform is actually handled by the Claude app behind the scenes, including permissions such as Full Disk Access. All apps made with Claude (either the ones you make, or the ones shared with you by other people) get installed at ~/Applications/Claude Apps, so they’re indexed by Spotlight and can be pinned to the macOS Dock. In fact, when you first create an app inside a Claude conversation (which can be a regular Claude session – you do not need to use Claude Code for these), there is a cute animation and install flow that puts an app directly in your Dock. It’s not too dissimilar from how the Shortcuts app can add individual shortcuts to your Mac’s Dock.

You can preview and install apps from Claude.

Crucially, these are **not** native apps created with Swift or SwiftUI: they’re HTML apps, wrapped inside an Electron shim, which is entirely managed by Claude’s Chromium process for Electron. It’s somewhat reminiscent of Raycast’s [Glaze](https://www.glaze.app/) product, which uses Vite/React web apps, rendered inside Apple’s [WKWebView](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/webkit/wkwebview), wrapped in a custom Swift shell. (Glaze also added the ability to [integrate native Swift modules](https://www.glaze.app/changelog/0-13-0-0) into their apps; I expect Anthropic to add this too.)

To test out this Claude feature, I wanted to create a disk analyzer utility with a menu bar companion for my Mac. The initial prompt was pure vibe coding:

> make me an artifact that analyzes disk space on my Mac with a stunning native Liquid Glass UI and install it in my dock

A few minutes later, Opus 5.5 made something that worked and installed it in my Dock, but it wasn’t great. So, I kept tweaking it. As Claude was working, I noticed that it kept editing a single index.html file:

How Claude makes “apps”.

When the app was done, I asked Claude Code to explain how the other Claude built the app. Here is the Claude Code explanation of it all:

> Storage Lens isn’t a traditional Mac app. Its 900 KB bundle holds no web code at all, just three pieces:
> A 51 KB Objective-C launcher, linked only against Cocoa and Foundation. It uses Electron’s “app shim” mechanism to find /Applications/Claude.app and load Claude’s copy of the Electron framework.
> An 80 KB notification helper built on UserNotifications. It won’t run unless it was launched by a signed Claude.app.
> An icon.
> What looks like a standalone app with its own Dock icon is really a Claude process in disguise.
> The app itself is a single HTML file, written by hand with no third-party frameworks: no React, no Tailwind, no D3. It’s plain JavaScript, with one state object and render() functions that rebuild the page. Everything visual is hand-made:
> The capacity ring is an SVG drawn with stroke-dasharray tricks.
> The treemap uses a hand-written squarified layout.
> The app icon is drawn on a <canvas> each time the app launches.
> The Liquid Glass look comes entirely from CSS: backdrop-filter, light-dark(), and color-mix(in oklab).
> The sliding toolbar highlight uses an SVG distortion filter whose map is generated pixel by pixel, so it bends the background like a real lens.
> The interesting part is how a web page gets to touch the file system. Storage Lens calls window.claude.use('desktop'), an API that closely mirrors Electron’s own: childProcess.spawn, fs.readdir, shell.trashItem, Menu.setApplicationMenu, app.dock.setBadge. With that, it runs the same command-line tools a power user would:
> df -kP and diskutil for volumes
> du -k -x -d 2 for folder sizes
> mdfind with a kMDItemFSSize query for large files
> It reads their output line by line as they run and caches the results in localStorage. Nothing leaves the Mac.

…

items.title: Hera spacecraft gets 1st up-close look at stadium-sized hole punched in asteroid by NASA DART mission
items.subtitle: NASA's DART Earth-defense mission punched a stadium-sized hole in a distant asteroid, and we have seen it up close for the first time thanks to the…
items.feedText: NASA's DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) mission made history on Sept. 26, 2022, when it slammed into Dimorphos, the small moonlet of the much larger asteroid Didymos. The mission tested if such an impact could be deployed to divert an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. items.body:
NASA's DART Earth-defense mission punched a stadium-sized hole in a distant asteroid, and we have seen it up close for the first time thanks to the Hera spacecraft.

NASA's [DART](https://www.space.com/dart-asteroid-mission) (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) mission made history on Sept. 26, 2022, when it slammed into [Dimorphos](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/asteroid-comet-missions/dimorphos-in-sight-europes-hera-probe-gets-its-1st-look-at-battered-space-rock-photo), the small moonlet of the much larger asteroid [Didymos](https://www.space.com/didymos-asteroid-facts). The mission tested if such an impact could be deployed to divert an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. Scientists have known for some time that this deflection attempt was successful; the system's orbit around [the sun](https://www.space.com/58-the-sun-formation-facts-and-characteristics.html) was lengthened by 33 minutes, but the European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera mission launched in October 2024 to travel the 120 million miles (194 million kilometers) to the Didymos system to observe the effect of the DART impact in greater detail.

Now, the spacecraft has revealed that DART flattened one face of Dimorphos with a stadium-sized crater and set it tumbling chaotically. The impact also appears to have blasted out hundreds of previously unknown boulders that are now circling the binary asteroids.

"Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape, or stayed the same," Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at the Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, said in a statement.

"Much to our surprise, the answer turns out to be all three at once! The face struck by DART has been flattened into an impact crater the size of a sports stadium, which extends across the asteroid's entire width."

## An important step for Earth defence

Michael Kueppers, ESA's Hera mission scientist, detailed some of the changes to the impacted moonlet seen by the spacecraft: "As Hera returned more images, it became clear that the DART impact has left Dimorphos tumbling wildly in its orbit.

"Another big surprise is that Hera is showing that the asteroids are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders, just a few meters in size."

It wasn't all change for Dimorphos. Hera discovered that the boulder fields covering the regions of the moonlet not impacted look just like they did when DART imaged it in 2022.

(Left) Didymos system seen by DART in 2022 (Right): the same system seen by Hera in 2026 (Image credit: ESA/NASA)

[Hera](https://www.space.com/hera-asteroid-mission-earth-moon-images) isn't finished with Didymos and its moonlet. The ESA spacecraft is currently in a rectangular orbit around the asteroid binary system, using its thrusters to maintain a distance of around 18.6 miles (30 kilometers). This allows Hera to continue observing Didymos and Dimorphos.

Hera will soon come to within around 8 miles (13 km) of the asteroids, capturing even more detailed images of the space rocks. Following this, it will deploy two showbox-sized [CubeSats](https://www.space.com/34324-cubesats.html), which will get even closer to the asteroids.

The CubeSat Juventas will use low-frequency radar to probe the interior of Dimorphos, the first time this has ever been done for an asteroid, and will eventually attempt to land on the moonlet to measure its gravity. Meanwhile, the Milani CubeSat will prospect asteroid materials and dust around the Didymos system.

Together, Hera and its CubeSats will more precisely determine the mass of Dimorphos, which, when combined with information about the orbital change of the system, will be crucial in planning missions to deflect threatening asteroids.

An infrared view of Didymos as seen by Hera (Image credit: ESA)

Hera's observations were revealed on Wednesday (Nov. 25) at the dinosaur hall of the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin, Germany. That location isn't a coincidence: It is a stark reminder of why this planetary defense mission is so important. Especially if humanity doesn't want to go the way of the [dinosaurs](https://www.space.com/astronomy/asteroids/the-asteroid-that-wiped-out-the-dinosaurs-may-have-created-a-vast-underground-habitat-for-life-that-lasted-8-million-years), whose rule on Earth ended when an asteroid fell from the sky.

"Sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid impact changed the course of life on Earth. Today, for the first time in history, humanity is validating how to prevent such an event from happening again," Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli explained. "NASA's DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid's orbit. Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself.

"By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet."

items.title: ALMA Reveals a Dying Star's Final Breath, Encoded In a Giant Ring of Gas
items.subtitle: About 6,500 years ago, a dying star emitted its final thermal pulse.
items.feedText: That dying breath created a giant ring of gas detected by ALMA. Then only 700 years ago, the star formed an hourglass nebula. Theory predicted this, but this is the first direct evidence supporting it.
items.body:
# ALMA Reveals a Dying Star's Final Breath, Encoded In a Giant Ring of Gas

Stars transition through different stages as they evolve. Sun-like stars with low to intermediate masses (about 0.8 to 8 solar masses) begin as main-sequence stars, then transition sequentially to red giants, asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, then post-AGB stars. By the end, they leave behind only a planetary nebula . Each of those transitions are detailed and complicated, and astrophysicists crave a more complete understanding of them.

Stars in their AGB phase have an important job. They spread heavy elements into the surrounding interstellar medium (ISM) and those elements are taken up in subsequent star and planet formation. As they transition from AGB phase to post-AGB phase, they experience thermal pulses that expel material. These events are like brief snapshots in the long life of a star, and catching one in the act is challenging.

Astronomers working with the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) have caught a star after what seems to be its final thermal pulse, leaving behing a planetary nebula. This is a rare opportunity to study this transition in detail.

> “We’ve caught, for the first time, a star’s final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas.” - Raghvendra Sahai, NASA/JPL.

Their observations are in new research titled " The Last Gasps of a Dying Star: ALMA Observations of the Preplanetary Nebula IRAS 06530–0213 ." It's published in The Astrophysical Journal, and the lead author is Raghvendra Sahai, senior research scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

IRAS 06530–0213 is a preplanetary nebula (PPN) about 12,000 light years away. Astronomers have been watching it for years as it takes shape. They know that the preplanetary nebula phase is a critical evolutionary stage in a star's transition from the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stage to the planetary nebula (PN) stage. PPN structures contain critical insights that aren't available in any other way.

"These data show the presence of an extended circular ring—first evidence of the last thermal pulse preceding the post-asymptotic giant branch (AGB) phase in a carbon star—and a central bipolar nebula (CBN) and torus," the authors write. The outer ring came from the last thermal pulse about 6500 years ago, and is the first direct evidence of this type of thermal pulse that's emitted before a star like this begins its final phase.

This snapshot is all about the mass-loss stars experience as they die, and the authors explain that the AGB progenitor's mass-loss rate "decreased immediately after the thermal pulse, then rose again just before the post-AGB phase."

The mass-loss dropped off for about 2,000 years, then for about 1,000 years after that, it rose again. The filamentary structures around around the CBN are evidence of the star emitting a thick and lumpy shell of gas. An hourglass-shaped nebula with a torus is inside the filamentary arc region.

This ALMA image of IRAS 06530 show the PPN's structure. The outer molecular ring is from its progenitor star's final thermal pulse. The CBN is the central bipolar nebula, and the FAR is the filamentary arc region. The FAR is evidence of the progenitor's mass loss rate dropping immediately after the thermal pulse, then rising again just before the star's post-AGB phase. Image Credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO); Sahai et al. (2026)

Based on the expansion ages of the torus and the CBN, Sahai and his co-researchers determined that the progenitor star transitioned to a post-AGB star around only 700 yrs ago, maybe a little less than that. That is a remarkably short amount of time to have lapsed since its transition, considering stellar ages.

In 2003 it was first identified as a carbon-rich PPN, and its envelope expansion velocity was measured. Subsequent research identified its s-process enrichment, where elements heavier than iron are synthesized. Then in 2025, this paper identified the PPN's spherical halo and central barrel-shaped torus.

Luck might not describe these most recent observations, because those prior observations were the primer, but good fortune might. The kind of good fortune that finds its way to people who spend their lives watching stars.

“Most of us think of stars as unchanging points of light, but this is a real-time snapshot of a star’s death throes,” said lead author Sahai, author and co-author of more than 140 published papers. “It’s the brief, violent transition between a bloated red giant and a glowing planetary nebula, frozen mid-action.”

There is something puzzling in this PPN and its filamentary arc region that still needs an explanation. "The arc stuctures are likely part of a 3D Archimedean spiral structure generally attributed to the presence of a binary companion," the authors write.

This image shows the central region of IRAS 06530, showing filamentary arc structures with dashed green, cyan, and white arcs. These arcs are typical signatures of a binary companion, but the researchers didn't fine one. Image Credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO); Sahai et al. (2026)

Dying stars with companions not only have spiral structures, but they're normally found inside compact dust disks. The disks are evidence of mass-transfer with a close binary companion. The mass-transfer is usually the cause of the hourglass-shapes. But the researchers didn't find a dusty disk, the usual signature of a companion.

"However, we do not find a compact continuum source at the location of IRAS 06530’s central star, such as that associated with the compact dusty disks typically found in disk-prominent post-AGB objects known to have binary companions," the researchers explain.

“Dying stars so often have hidden companions that reshape their ejected material into intricate, bipolar or multipolar forms instead of simple spheres,” said Sahai. “IRAS 06530 shows that the story is more complicated than the tidy explanation we’ve been using.”

items.body:
After backlash from sellers frustrated by Etsy’s new AI policies, which appeared to allow the company to train AI on user artwork, Etsy has now clarified its stance.

In a note [published](https://www.etsy.com/news/etsyas-terms-of-use?ref=news) on Monday, CEO Kruti Patel Goyal discussed recent tweaks to the company's terms of service and admitted that her team "should’ve given you more context on what the updates meant for your creative content."

“Our recent terms update was meant to reflect the evolving technologies we're using to build better tools and experiences for sellers and the Etsy community,” Goyal wrote this week. “It was not meant to enable us to train AI models for the purpose of creating copycats of your items. We do not and will not do that.”

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026/11/etsy-clarifies-ai-terms-after-seller-backlash/)

[Comments](https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2026/11/etsy-clarifies-ai-terms-after-seller-backlash/#comments)
